lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.grammar: Ee / Mba (yes / no) and polite words like biko (please).
lessons.objective: Can greet people, thank them, and say goodbye.

items.cultural_note: Used especially with elders or strangers — shows respect from the first word.
Gratitude is central to Igbo etiquette. "Daalụ nke ọma" (thank you very much) signals deep appreciation.
A warm farewell blessing — "hold (your) strength."

items.tone_note: Egwu here uses high-high tone (music/amazement), distinct from low-high tone meaning fear.

lessons.title: People & introductions
lessons.grammar: Subject pronouns m, ị, ọ, anyị, unu, ha. "Aha m bụ ___" = "My name is ___."
lessons.objective: Can use subject pronouns and say your own name.

items.cultural_note: Igbo names carry deep meaning — "Amara" means grace. Asking names is one of the first social rituals.
Friendship (enyi) is a social pillar — age-grade groups (otu) form lifelong bonds.
"Igbo bu otu" — "Igbo is one." Mmadụ (person) sits at the heart of Igbo humanist philosophy.

items.tone_note: Tone-distinguished from Eze meaning tooth/teeth in the body lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers 1–10
lessons.objective: Can count from 1 to 10.

items.cultural_note: Igbo counting is base-10, but market prices traditionally used cowrie shells.

lessons.title: Numbers 11–20
lessons.grammar: Pattern: iri na + number (ten and + number). Twenty = iri abụọ (two tens).
lessons.objective: Can count from 11 to 20.

items.example_sentence: Ha nwere iri abụọ ụmụ akwụkwọ.

lessons.title: Family
lessons.grammar: Nouns. Possession ("my mother") comes a little later.
lessons.objective: Can name immediate and extended family members.

items.cultural_note: Nne (mother) is also a term of endearment for older women you respect.
Nna (father) is also an honorific for respected elder men. The family compound (obi) belongs to the Nna figure.
Children (nwa) carry the family name and ancestral lineage forward.
Nwaanyị play a central role in Igbo economy — women historically dominated the market (ahịa) and trade networks.

items.example_sentence: Nwanne m bụ enyi m kacha mma.

items.cultural_note: "Old mother" — grandmothers are the keepers of Igbo oral tradition and proverbs.
Ụmụnna (fathers\' children) — the extended patrilineal clan that shares land, names, and responsibility.

lessons.title: Food & drink
lessons.objective: Can name common foods and drinks.

items.example_sentence: Ji bụ eze ọjị n\'ala Igbo.
items.cultural_note: The yam is the king of crops in Igbo culture. The New Yam Festival (Iri Ji Ọhụrụ) is one of the most sacred annual celebrations.

items.example_sentence: M chọrọ anụ na nri m.

items.cultural_note: Fish (azụ) is a staple protein in Igbo cooking, especially dried or smoked in soups.
Leafy greens like ugu (fluted pumpkin) and oha are staples in Igbo soups. Akwụkwọ nri literally means "leaf food."
The kola nut (ọjị) is sacred in Igbo culture. "Onye wetara ọjị wetara ndụ" — "He who brings kola brings life."
Palm wine (mmanya ngwo) is a traditional fermented drink central to Igbo ceremonies.

lessons.title: Common verbs
lessons.grammar: Verbs cited with the i-/ị- infinitive prefix; root carries the meaning.
lessons.objective: Can recognise and use everyday verbs.

items.note: As in "iri nri" — to eat food.

items.tone_note: Requires ṅ (U+1E45 velar nasal). Distinct from Ịnụ (to hear) — verify font renders ṅ correctly.

items.example_sentence: Ọ sụrụ asụsụ Igbo nke ọma.
items.cultural_note: "Ịsụ asụsụ Igbo" is more than communication — it is an act of cultural identity.
items.note: As in "ịsụ asụsụ" — to speak a language.

items.tone_note: Plain n — distinct from Ịṅụ (to drink) which uses velar nasal ṅ.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.grammar: Question words usually open the sentence.
lessons.objective: Can ask simple question-word questions.

items.example_sentence: Otú ọ dị, ọ dị mma?

lessons.title: The body
lessons.objective: Can name the main parts of the human body.

items.cultural_note: Anya (eye) also appears in the word for love: ịhụnanya — literally "to see with love."

items.tone_note: Standard spelling is Ntị (with ị), not Nti.

items.cultural_note: "Obi" also means the main hall of the family compound — the emotional and physical centre of a household.

items.tone_note: Same spelling as Afọ (year) and Afọ (market day) — tone-distinguished.

items.cultural_note: Blood (ọbara) is central to Igbo kinship and sacrifice traditions.

items.tone_note: Tone-distinguished from Eze meaning king (people lesson).
Same romanisation as Azụ (fish) in the food lesson — tone-distinguished.
Carries both neck and voice meanings — tone-distinguished.

lessons.title: Time & days
lessons.grammar: Time words often precede the sentence they modify.
lessons.objective: Can describe when something happens.

items.tone_note: Correctly translated as night, not evening. Evening = Mgbede.
Double-a is correct standard Onwu spelling.
Same spelling as Afọ (belly) and Afọ (market day) — tone-distinguished.

items.cultural_note: New-moon nights marked community gatherings.
items.tone_note: Same word for both month and moon — dual meaning reflects the lunar calendar.

items.cultural_note: Traditional Igbo week has 4 days: Eke, Orie, Afọ, Nkwọ. These cycle and define local identity.

items.note: Variant of Anyasị — both are widely used for night/darkness.

lessons.title: Places
lessons.objective: Can name and describe common places.

items.cultural_note: The market (ahịa) is the social and economic heart of Igbo communities — historically women-run.
The forest (ọhịa) in Igbo cosmology is home to spirits and medicines — a place of power and respect.
Obodo encompasses your hometown and the broader nation — "Obodo Igbo" means Igboland.
Ala (earth/land) is also the Igbo earth goddess — arguably the most important deity in traditional religion.

lessons.title: Feelings & emotions
lessons.objective: Can express basic emotions.

items.cultural_note: "Sweet heart" — Igbo expressions for joy are often heart-centred.

items.note: Conversational phrase for a bad or heavy heart — less formal than Mwute.

items.tone_note: Low-high tone = fear. High-high tone = music/dance. Audio required to distinguish.

items.cultural_note: Ịhụnanya — "to see with (eyes of) love." The word for love contains anya (eye): to love is to see deeply.
"Slowly, slowly" — patience (nwayọọ) is deeply valued in Igbo culture.

lessons.title: Nature & animals
lessons.objective: Can name elements of nature and common animals.

items.cultural_note: Anyanwụ literally means "eye of light" — anya (eye) + anwụ (light/fire). A poetic Igbo compound.

items.tone_note: Same word as Ọnwa (month) — dual meaning reflecting the lunar calendar.

items.cultural_note: Igwe means sky, but also iron and the title for a king. The sky-king connection is ancient.
items.tone_note: Multiple meanings — tone-distinguished. Also a title for a king.
Same spelling as Ọkụ (hot/adjective) — tone-distinguished.

items.note: Standard Igbo; dialectal variant is Okoko osisi.

items.tone_note: Also means book/paper — context-distinguished.

items.note: Standard form; Efi is a dialectal variant.

items.cultural_note: Goats (ewu) are the most common sacrificial animal in Igbo ceremonies. "Ewu ojii" (black goat) carries special ritual significance.
The lion (odụm) symbolises royalty and courage in Igbo proverbs.

lessons.title: Describing things
lessons.grammar: Adjectives in Igbo typically follow the noun they modify.
lessons.objective: Can describe basic qualities of nouns.

items.note: Colloquial/diminutive — more emphatic than Obere. Also used as an adverb meaning "a little."

items.cultural_note: Ochie carries reverence — "omenala ochie" (old customs) refers to sacred ancestral traditions.

items.tone_note: Tone-distinguished from Ike (power/strength as noun) and Ike (buttocks).

items.cultural_note: Ọcha implies purity in both physical and spiritual senses — ritually clean objects are called "ihe ọcha."

items.tone_note: Same spelling as Ọkụ (fire/noun) — tone-distinguished.

lessons.title: Home & objects
lessons.objective: Can name common household objects and items of clothing.

items.tone_note: Also means leaf — context-distinguished.

lessons.title: School & learning
lessons.objective: Can talk about school, learning, and language.

lessons.title: Community & daily life
lessons.objective: Can describe everyday community life and activities.

lessons.title: Abstract concepts
lessons.objective: Can express abstract ideas about life, belief, and values.

items.cultural_note: Chi is your personal spirit and destiny — deeply embedded in Igbo worldview.

items.tone_note: Tone-distinguished from Ike (adjective: strong/hard) and Ike (buttocks).
High-high tone = music/dance. Low-high tone = fear. Audio required to distinguish.

lessons.title: Market & Salutations
lessons.grammar: Ọma ("good") follows a time-of-day noun to form a greeting: Ụtụtụ + ọma = good morning.
lessons.objective: Can bargain in the market and use time-specific and respectful greetings.

items.note: The most common price question — pairs with Ole (how much/many) in the Questions lesson.

items.igbo: Achọrọ m ihe dị ọnụ ala

items.note: Polite way to end negotiation without buying.
Time-specific greeting variant — complements Ka chi fo in the Greetings lesson.
Pairs with Abalị (night) in the Time & Days lesson.
Respectful address term — the same word literally means "father" (see Family lesson); context distinguishes.
Respectful address term — the same word literally means "mother" (see Family lesson); context distinguishes.

items.cultural_note: Also the title given to a first daughter.

items.note: Warm peer-to-peer address — extends Nwanne (sibling) from the Family lesson.

items.cultural_note: A call-and-response shout at gatherings and ceremonies, traditionally answered "Yaa!" by the crowd — one of the most recognisable public expressions in Igbo culture.
Where communal gatherings, dispute resolution, and proverbs are traditionally spoken.

lessons.title: Proverbs
lessons.objective: Can understand and explain 13 core Igbo proverbs and their cultural meaning.
